title: The Teachers Job Is Six Jobs
author: Michael Connell
summary: Michael Connell uses an open house at Alpha School Boston to examine why parents keep asking what the adults there actually do. He argues that the questions fixate on visible features, such as the title guide, instead of the system function each feature serves. Using a dinner party analogy and the history of factory electrification, he shows that new technology pays off only when surrounding structures are redesigned. His central analysis is that the traditional teacher bundles six functions: curriculum design, instruction, assessment, motivational coaching, administration and parent communication. Mastery-based software can now take over instruction, which lets the guide specialize in coaching and frees time for applied life-skills work. He then traces how unbundling would ripple through hiring, scheduling, testing, district operations and costs. The piece moves from a local anecdote to a systems claim that the real innovation lies in questioning why functions were bundled, not in AI as such.
points: The classroom teacher's job bundles six distinct functions, and the bundle persisted mainly because no practical way existed to separate them.
Alpha's guide is best read as a teacher whose instruction duty moved to software, leaving time for motivational coaching, not as a teacher replaced by AI.
Mastery-based software compresses academic time, shifting the school day toward applied life-skills projects where peer interaction happens.
Unbundling the teacher simplifies hiring, scheduling, certification, testing and administration at school and district levels, and could lower cost.
A single classroom adopting software gains little unless the wider system changes, like an electric motor installed to drive an old shaft.
quotes: The central constraint was that, until quite recently, there was no practical way to unbundle the different aspects of this complex role. If you have one adult, thirty children, a textbook, and a chalkboard (or these days a smartboard), then instruction has to come from the adult, and if instruction comes from the adult, assessment and record-keeping more or less have to as well, because the adult is the only one who knows what was taught and who has seen the students’ work.
When a new capability arrives at one level, the incremental value it can deliver is boxed in by the assumptions held fixed at the others.

The economist Paul David, writing about this episode, argued that the benefits of a new technology come mostly from the organizational redesign it enables, and that the redesign can take decades because people first have to recognize that they no longer need to work around the old bottlenecks.

A role that no longer delivers instruction is reasonably given a different name, which is why the adult in the room is called a guide. Note that nothing on the list has disappeared. Each function is still being performed, and arguably performed better, by a component designed for it.

One of the guides at the open house told me that she had spent her career in public schools, and that what she had always most wanted to do was the motivational coaching (connecting with each kid and figuring out how to help that particular kid thrive). There was almost no time for it, she said, because the rest of the duties on the list took up nearly all of her day. Motivational coaching is now her full-time job, as it is for guides at Alpha generally and in many microschool models. In terms of the dinner party, she is the host who has finally been let out of the kitchen.

The short version is that a great deal of the complexity at the school and district levels exists to support the bundled teacher, so unbundling the teacher creates an opportunity to simplify those levels too.

Suppose a single public school classroom adopts excellent mastery-based software tomorrow. The teacher is still certified, hired, scheduled, and evaluated as a deliverer of whole-class instruction. The students are still grouped by age and expected to move through the year’s material on the year’s calendar. The state test still arrives in the spring, and the teacher is still accountable for it. Under those conditions the software becomes one more thing for the teacher to manage, which is the electric motor installed in the basement, driving the old shaft.

This is why I would argue that perhaps the core innovation of models like Alpha and some microschools is not their use of technology or AI per se but their willingness to revisit the assumptions that bundled these functions together in the first place, at every level simultaneously, and to set up a different ecosystem that can take advantage of the new opportunities that open up across the different levels when the role is unbundled.
context: Connell explains why one role came to hold six functions, which sets up his claim that technology now allows them to be separated.
He states the structural problem that makes change hard, since each level of the school hierarchy limits what a new capability can deliver.
The factory electrification history gives him a precedent for the idea that gains come from organizational redesign and not the technology alone.
This passage answers the parents' naming question by treating the guide as a redistributed role rather than a missing one.
A veteran teacher's testimony supplies human evidence that the refactored role frees time for the coaching many teachers entered the profession to do.
He claims that much of the machinery above the classroom exists to support the bundled teacher, so unbundling reaches the whole system.
He explains why piecemeal adoption fails, since the old hiring, scheduling and accountability rules still govern the teacher.
His thesis is that the core innovation is revisiting why functions were bundled across every level, with technology as an enabler.
